opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic issue is that language is fundamentally discrete. Diffusion models were really designed for continuous data like images, where you can add a little bit of Gaussian noise to a pixel value and it still makes sense. You're moving smoothly through a continuous space. With text you have tokens, and there's no natural notion of adding a little bit of noise to the word "cat."

So one natural idea people tried was to map tokens into a continuous embedding space and then run a standard continuous diffusion process there. The trouble is that it creates a whole set of new problems. First, you have to learn or choose the embedding, and it's not obvious what a good one looks like. If you learn it jointly with the diffusion model, you can get collapse issues, where the embeddings shrink together or become degenerate, because that makes the denoising objective easy. Then at the end of generation you have to round from a continuous vector back to a discrete token. That rounding step is a source of errors, and small mistakes in the continuous space can turn into the wrong word.

More broadly, most of the embedding space doesn't correspond to anything meaningful. The real data lives on a very sparse set of points, and the model spends a lot of capacity modeling the space in between. Empirically, these embedding-space approaches have struggled to match autoregressive models on perplexity and sample quality, and they often need tricks like self-conditioning or clamping to work.

That's really what motivated us to work directly in the discrete space instead. In our work on discrete diffusion, for example with score entropy, we define the noising process over the tokens themselves, like randomly replacing tokens or masking them. Then we learn the analog of the score function for discrete data, which turns out to be ratios of probabilities between neighboring sequences. That avoids the embedding and rounding problems entirely, and we found it closes much of the gap with autoregressive models. It also keeps the nice properties of diffusion, like generating many tokens in parallel and trading compute for quality.

r001.rationale: The response says continuous embeddings must be rounded back to discrete tokens, and that small errors in continuous space can produce the wrong word.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core difficulty is that language is fundamentally discrete, and diffusion models were really built for continuous data. With images, you have pixels that live on a continuum, so adding Gaussian noise and then learning to reverse that process is very natural. The noise is small, the perturbations are meaningful, and the model can gradually denoise.

With text, you don't have that. A token is either "cat" or it isn't. So the obvious workaround, which a lot of people tried early on, is to map tokens into some continuous embedding space, run the diffusion process there, and then at the end round each denoised vector back to the nearest token. And that sounds reasonable, but in practice it creates a few problems.

The first is this rounding step. You're doing diffusion in a continuous space, but the thing you actually care about lives on a tiny discrete set of points inside that space. Most of the volume you're denoising through doesn't correspond to any valid word. So the model spends a lot of capacity learning to navigate regions that are essentially meaningless, and then you have this abrupt, lossy snap to a token at the end. Small errors in the continuous space can flip you to a completely different word, and because words aren't arranged in embedding space in any way that makes nearby points semantically interchangeable in a controlled fashion, that error doesn't degrade gracefully the way blurring an image does.

The second issue is that the embedding space itself is a design choice, and it's not clear what the right one is. If you learn it jointly, there's a tendency for the embeddings to collapse or to drift in ways that make the denoising task trivially easy or badly conditioned. If you fix them, say from a pretrained model, you're imposing a geometry that was never designed with a diffusion process in mind. And the noise schedule, which is so important in image diffusion, doesn't have an obvious analog. What does it mean to add a "little" noise to the word "the"?

And then third, more pragmatically, you lose a lot of the machinery that makes autoregressive language models work so well. The likelihood becomes awkward to define because of that rounding step, so you can't really do clean maximum likelihood training or compare perplexities, and you don't naturally get the kind of scaling behavior we've seen with transformers trained on next-token prediction.

So that's actually what pushed us toward thinking about diffusion directly in the discrete space, where you define a corruption process over tokens themselves, masking them or replacing them, and you learn to reverse that. You stay on the manifold of valid sequences the whole time, you can write down a proper likelihood bound, and you avoid this mismatch between a continuous process and a discrete target. I think the embedding-space approach was a very natural first thing to try, but the mismatch between the data type and the modeling assumptions was really the central obstacle.

r001.rationale: The response explains that denoised vectors may not correspond to valid words and must be rounded to the nearest token, making decoding lossy and error-prone.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difficulty is that language is discrete, whereas diffusion models work very naturally with continuous data. You can map tokens into an embedding space and add noise there, but then you have to ask whether the geometry of that space is actually appropriate for generation. If two embeddings are close, does that mean they represent words that are interchangeable in a particular context? Not necessarily.

And at the end, you have to map the continuous output back to discrete tokens. You can have a small error in embedding space that changes which token you decode, and that can make a big difference to the meaning of a sentence. So the challenge is finding a representation where the continuous denoising problem lines up well with the discrete language generation problem. Just moving into an embedding space doesn’t automatically resolve that mismatch.

r001.rationale: The response says a small embedding-space error can change which token is decoded, conveying the difficulty that generated embeddings may not land exactly on a dictionary-word embedding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main difficulty is that language is discrete, whereas diffusion models naturally operate in a continuous space. You can map tokens into embeddings and do diffusion there, but then you have to map the result back to actual tokens. And that mapping can be quite sensitive: two points that are close in embedding space don’t necessarily correspond to interchangeable words or to sentences with the same meaning.

So you’re really asking the model to solve two problems: learn the distribution in that continuous space, and produce samples that decode into coherent language. The choice of embedding space, and how you connect the diffusion process to the discrete output, becomes really important.

r001.rationale: The response notes that generated embeddings must be mapped back to tokens and that this mapping can be sensitive, but it does not say they may fail to land exactly on an embedding corresponding to a dictionary word.
